judgments.move: Give every graphic one job tied to this product: show an input becoming a state change and a result, show a real relationship between real objects, or carry a recurring brand grammar through the page; drop treatments that pass the swap test, and order sections so the visual story depends on the sequence.
judgments.why: Treatments combined without a product relationship read as a template even when polished; graphics that encode this product's mechanism cannot be swapped and make the page recognisably authored.
judgments.notWhen: Purely atmospheric fields whose stated job is rhythm or mood between information sections; screenshot-led pages whose product UI already carries the specificity; brand systems whose recurring abstract grammar is itself the identity.

judgments.look: A section graphic that places several symbols at equal weight (a window, an icon, a cursor, a badge, a mascot) so none of them states the section's claim; or a polished scene a visitor admires without being able to say what it shows; or a stock symbol for one word of the headline (a magnifier, a rocket, a lightbulb) standing in for what the product does.
judgments.ask: Covering the headline, can a visitor say from the picture alone what this section claims, and is there exactly one thing the eye lands on first?
judgments.move: Pick the single moment the headline describes, make its key noun the protagonist and enlarge, lift and colour it; push every supporting element back into context by greying, blurring, cropping or reducing it to a skeleton. Use the product's real vocabulary — actual commands, values, state names — on the protagonist. Show the change this product makes, as it happens in this product, rather than describe it. The protagonist is real material from the product or an object that acts out its mechanism, never an invented example site, filler copy or placeholder shapes; words inside the art are only the labels its objects carry, and art that holds more words than its section copy explains nothing.
judgments.why: A designer's feature graphic is an argument with one subject; equal-weight symbols read as decoration and leave the reader to guess the point.
judgments.notWhen: Purely atmospheric fields between information sections; a real product screenshot or footage whose own content already isolates the subject.

judgments.look: Graphics built from flat fills and hairline outlines that sit on the page like diagrams; or the opposite, heavy 3D models in every section that overwhelm the message and the brand.
judgments.ask: Where the art direction wants depth, does it come from light on mostly 2D forms — and is any modelled 3D reserved for a recurring accent?
judgments.move: Give the protagonist volume with light rather than geometry: a gradient fill, an inner top highlight, a colour-matched soft shadow, a glow field behind it, a slight tilt, and blur on the layers behind; let one or two shapes overlap or break the frame. Keep rendered 3D for a brand character or object that recurs, not for every scene.
judgments.why: Polished product sites read as deep and tactile mostly through lit 2D shapes; flat diagrams look unfinished and wall-to-wall 3D looks like a stock icon pack.
judgments.notWhen: Deliberately flat, editorial or technical brands; documentation and product UI, where depth effects compete with content.

judgments.look: A gradient used as paint: an even linear wash across a section, a symmetric glow blob centred behind the headline, or a purple-to-pink rainbow that repeats identically in every section and could be deleted without losing anything.
judgments.ask: Does each gradient behave like a light source in the space — with a direction, a soft falloff into the base tone and an edge it catches — within one hue family, and does where it falls lead the eye to the content it lights?
judgments.move: Treat the base as a dark or pale room and the gradient as light entering it: large, soft and off-centre, raking from one side, fading into the base rather than filling it. Stay in one hue family and vary luminance; move the light's position from section to section for rhythm and let it leak across a section edge or catch a word, a rule or a card edge. Add fine grain so the falloff does not band, and keep body text on the calm part of the field.
judgments.why: Designers use gradients as light, which gives depth, mood and direction; gradients used as fills read as a generated template and flatten the page.
judgments.notWhen: Product UI and dense reading surfaces; brands whose palette is deliberately flat; sections where a photograph already supplies the light.

judgments.look: The page is correct and readable but could introduce any product in its category: the hero states a promise over a decorative scene, proof is a row of round numbers or logos nobody can check, feature art is a picture about the product rather than the product doing something, and every state shown is the happy one.
judgments.ask: Placed on the ladder template → clean → considered → memorable, does this page reach considered: would the brief's primary persona, within five seconds of the hero, see this product act on something realistic and believe the thing they came to check?
judgments.move: Start from the brief's primary persona and their five-second belief. Put that proof in the hero: the product working on a representative input with its consequence visible (a choice and its result, a request and what came back), or its real output, using specific realistic content rather than round invented figures. Where the product has them, show one state beyond the happy path — pending, needs attention, empty, a limit — because trust is decided there. Give the primary action one clear rank, make proof checkable (conditions, named sources, the real output) and let motion explain a change rather than decorate an entrance. Memorable is one well-made idea only this product could have, on top of that.
judgments.why: Before/after critiques of generated pages keep finding the same gap: the 'before' is clean but generic and its proof is made up; the 'after' answers one named visitor's question with the product visibly working on realistic data, including a failure or pending state. Rating the level first keeps twenty small polish notes from hiding that the page never shows the product.
judgments.notWhen: Products with nothing to operate or output on screen (a physical service, a policy), where real photographs or the real artifact and plain conditions carry the proof; never simulate a mechanism the product does not have.
